opus-5.5.text:
I think evaluation is becoming one of the central problems in the field, and honestly it's getting harder, not easier, as the models get stronger.

In the earlier days, most benchmarks were single-turn: a question goes in, an answer comes out, you check whether it matches. That's relatively clean. But once you move to end-to-end tasks, like an agent that browses, writes code, calls tools, and runs for dozens or hundreds of steps, a few things break down.

First, the outcome space becomes huge. For a real task, like "do a research report on this market" or "fix this bug in a large codebase," there isn't one correct answer. There are many acceptable trajectories and many acceptable final outputs. So you can't just do string matching. You need some judgment of quality, and that judgment is itself expensive and often subjective.

Second, there's the credit assignment problem. If a long task fails, where did it fail? Was it planning, a wrong tool call at step thirty, or a misunderstanding of the user's intent at the very beginning? A single pass-or-fail score tells you very little about what to improve. For research purposes you want a much finer-grained signal.

Third, the environment itself becomes part of the evaluation. When the model interacts with web pages, operating systems, or real software, the environment is noisy and changes over time. Reproducibility suffers. The same model can score differently on different days for reasons that have nothing to do with the model.

And then there's a deeper issue: benchmarks saturate very quickly now. Once a benchmark becomes popular, people optimize toward it, sometimes explicitly, sometimes implicitly through data. The number goes up, but it doesn't necessarily mean the model is more useful to real users. So there's a growing gap between leaderboard progress and the experience people actually have.

My view is that evaluation and training are increasingly the same problem. If you can build a good verifier or a good environment for a task, you can usually also use it for reinforcement learning. So the ability to define what "good" means for a complex task is a core capability for a model company. It's not just a measurement step at the end; it shapes what the model becomes.

Practically, I think you need a combination: some carefully designed hard benchmarks that are verifiable, a lot of internal real-world task sets that reflect what users actually do, and human judgment from people with real taste in the domain. None of these alone is sufficient. And you have to keep refreshing them, because whatever you measure, the model will eventually get good at, and then you need to look for the next thing that's still hard.

r001.rationale: The response says end-to-end evaluation is getting harder and contrasts it with clean single-turn benchmarks, but it does not state that evaluation is harder than evaluating math problems or programming tasks with test cases.

fable-5.1.text:
I think evaluation is actually one of the hardest problems in the whole field right now, and it gets harder the more capable the models become.

When we were working on simple benchmarks, evaluation was cheap. You have a question, you have a reference answer, you check whether they match. But once you move to end-to-end tasks, things like completing a long coding project, doing a multi-step research task, or operating in a real software environment over hours, the structure of the problem changes completely. There is no single correct answer. There are many valid paths, and the quality of the outcome depends on judgment, on trade-offs, on whether the agent noticed something it wasn't explicitly told to look for.

So the first difficulty is just defining what "success" means. For a complex task, a human expert might take a long time to evaluate whether the result is actually good. That means the cost of a single evaluation sample is very high, and you can't easily scale it the way you scale pretraining data.

The second difficulty is that benchmarks saturate very fast. The moment a benchmark becomes popular, the whole community optimizes for it, and within months it stops telling you anything useful. For end-to-end tasks the problem is worse, because the tasks themselves tend to leak into training data, and the agent can learn surface patterns of the test environment rather than general capability.

The third issue, which I think is underappreciated, is that end-to-end tasks involve long horizons, and errors compound. A model that is ninety-five percent reliable per step looks very good on short benchmarks and terrible on a hundred-step task. So you need evaluations that actually measure robustness over long trajectories, not just accuracy at one moment.

My view is that the solution has to involve the model itself. We need to use strong models as judges, use environments with verifiable outcomes where possible, like code that either runs or doesn't, and build evaluation into the training loop rather than treating it as a separate step. In the long run, I think evaluation and reinforcement learning are really the same problem. If you can reliably tell whether a complex task was done well, you already have the reward signal you need to train the next generation. So whoever solves evaluation for complex tasks is, in some sense, solving the scaling problem for agents.

r001.rationale: The response says end-to-end evaluation is harder than evaluating simple benchmarks with reference answers, but it does not clearly identify math problems or programming tasks with test cases as the comparison.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part is defining what success actually means. For a narrow task, you can often check whether the answer is correct. But for an end-to-end task, like doing research or building a product, there are many reasonable outcomes, and the quality depends on a lot of intermediate decisions.

You also have to decide what you’re evaluating: the model itself, or the whole system, including its tools and the feedback it receives. A system might succeed with a lot of human guidance, but that’s different from completing the task independently. And two systems might both finish, but one takes ten times as long or costs ten times as much.

So I don’t think a single score is enough. You need realistic tasks, clear criteria for the final outcome, and repeated trials to understand reliability. Human judgment is still valuable, but it’s expensive and can be inconsistent. The challenge is making evaluation scalable without losing the things that make the task meaningful in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts end-to-end tasks with narrow tasks where correctness is easier to check, but it does not identify math or programming tasks with test cases as the comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that, for a complex end-to-end task, success is often hard to define, and even harder to measure automatically. If you ask a model a question with a clear answer, you can check whether it’s correct. But if you ask it to conduct research or build a product, there are many possible good outcomes. You have to evaluate the quality of the result, whether it satisfies the user’s intent, and sometimes how much human intervention was needed.

There’s also a diagnosis problem. A system might take dozens of steps and then fail. Was the issue reasoning, tool use, missing information, or an early mistake that propagated? A single score doesn’t tell you that.

So I think we need both end-to-end evaluation and more targeted evaluations. The end-to-end task tells us whether the system is actually useful, while the targeted tests help us understand what to improve. And we need to be careful that improvements on a benchmark translate into improvements in real use.

r001.rationale: The response says complex research or product tasks are harder to define and measure than questions with clear answers, but it does not compare them with math problems or programming tasks evaluated using test cases.
